enhanced.fullText:
The Higher Education Act's Misrepresentation provisions, codified at 20 U.S.C. § 1094 and implemented through 34 CFR § 668.71-668.75, establish comprehensive prohibitions against substantial misrepresentations by institutions participating in federal student aid programs. This regulation significantly expands institutional liability beyond direct institutional communications to include misrepresentations by institutional representatives, third-party marketers, recruiters, and any entity with whom the institution contracts for educational services, marketing, or admissions activities.

Under 34 CFR § 668.71(a), a substantial misrepresentation is defined as any false, erroneous, or misleading statement that has the likelihood or tendency to deceive or confuse students, prospective students, or persons acting on their behalf. The regulation covers three critical categories: (1) the nature of the educational program, including curriculum, faculty qualifications, facilities, equipment, and accreditation status; (2) the financial charges associated with enrollment, including tuition, fees, room and board, and other costs; and (3) the employability of graduates, including job placement rates, licensing exam pass rates, salary expectations, and career advancement opportunities.

Institutional responsibility extends to all communications made through any medium, including websites, social media, printed materials, oral presentations, and electronic communications. Per 34 CFR § 668.72, institutions must ensure accuracy in all representations regarding program outcomes, with particular scrutiny applied to gainful employment programs where specific disclosure requirements under 34 CFR § 668.412 mandate precise reporting of debt-to-earnings ratios and employment statistics.

Enforcement mechanisms under 20 U.S.C. § 1094(c)(3) and 34 CFR § 668.75 include progressive sanctions ranging from program reviews and compliance audits to limitation, suspension, or termination of federal student aid eligibility. The Department of Education may impose fines up to $55,907 per violation as of 2023 adjustments, require corrective advertisements, mandate student loan discharge provisions, and pursue recovery of federal funds. Recent amendments through the 2022 Federal Student Aid Handbook emphasize heightened scrutiny of digital marketing practices and social media advertising, requiring institutions to maintain comprehensive documentation of all promotional materials and third-party agreements for at least three years following publication or dissemination.
enhanced.summary: Federal regulation prohibiting substantial misrepresentations in higher education marketing, admissions, and program promotion. Institutions are liable for false statements by employees, contractors, and third parties regarding educational programs, costs, and employment outcomes.
enhanced.requirements:
## Institutional Oversight Requirements
- Implement comprehensive review processes for all marketing and recruitment materials
- Establish written policies governing third-party marketing agreements per 34 CFR § 668.72
- Conduct annual audits of promotional content accuracy and employment outcome representations
- Maintain documentation of all advertising materials for minimum three years

## Third-Party Management
- Execute written agreements with clear misrepresentation prohibitions for all contractors
- Implement regular monitoring of third-party marketing activities and communications
- Establish immediate corrective action protocols for identified misrepresentations

## Data Accuracy Standards
- Verify employment statistics and salary data before publication using verifiable sources
- Update program outcome information annually with current cohort data
- Implement fact-checking procedures for all public-facing educational program descriptions
enhanced.reportingRequirements: Institutions must immediately report suspected substantial misrepresentations to ED within 10 days of discovery per 34 CFR § 668.75(c). Annual compliance certifications required with federal student aid applications documenting adherence to misrepresentation prohibitions and third-party oversight activities.
